summary: NRDC's Composting 101 guide, written by Shelia Hu and dated July 20, 2020, explains how recycling organic waste into compost benefits the environment by cutting landfill methane, improving soil, conserving water and reducing food waste. It then gives practical guidance on home composting methods (cold, hot, bins, tumblers, trenches, vermicomposting), how to build a balanced pile, and what to keep out of compost such as pet waste, glossy paper, diseased plants and animal products.
one_line: NRDC guide explaining the environmental benefits of composting organic waste and how to compost at home, including methods, ingredients and items to avoid.
key_facts: Composting recycles food and other organic waste into compost, which provides environmental benefits including improved soil health, reduced greenhouse gas emissions, nutrient recycling, and mitigation of drought impacts.
Food scraps and garden waste combined make up more than 28 percent of what Americans throw away, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).
The average cost to landfill municipal solid waste in the United States was around $55 per ton in 2019.
Landfill biogas is roughly 50 percent methane and 50 percent carbon dioxide, and methane is 28 to 36 times more effective than CO2 at trapping heat over a century.
According to the EPA, landfills are the third-largest source of human-generated methane emissions in the United States.
Only about 6 percent of food waste gets composted, according to the source.
San Francisco established a large-scale composting program in 1996 and by 2000 diverted 50 percent of its waste from landfills; since 2012 it has diverted more than 80 percent.
Agriculture accounts for approximately 80 percent of the nation's water use, according to the EPA.
Each 1 percent increase in soil organic matter helps soil hold 20,000 gallons more water per acre.
An average American family of four throws out about $150 worth of food per month, a 50 percent increase since the 1970s.
The ideal carbon-to-nitrogen ratio for a compost pile is 25 to 30 parts carbon for every 1 part nitrogen.
The optimal peak temperature for aerobic hot composting is 130 to 140 degrees Fahrenheit.
The ideal compost pile size is a 3-foot cube, and piles larger than 5 cubic feet are not likely to allow enough air to reach the center.
Red wigglers are the best worm species for vermicomposting, and a typical home system needs about a pound of worms; vermicompost is produced in about three to six months.
Compost must reach and remain at a minimum of 131 degrees Fahrenheit for three consecutive days to kill pathogens found in pet waste, and cat or other pet waste should not be composted at home.
